text: `--abstain-if` is checked only when the assertion fails. When it holds, the record is an unsure: exit 7, and `"abstain": true` in place of `"assert": false`.
`--mock FILE`, or `ONESIE_MOCK=FILE` in the environment, answers from a file instead of the API. The gate, the exit codes, every output mode, `--out` and `--resume` run as they do for real.

`--resume` with `--id` skips answered records and asks the rest, failed ones included. A finished run rewrites the file in input order and keeps answered ids the input no longer has, unless `--prune` drops them. A changed fingerprint refuses with exit 2. A record whose content changed but whose id did not keeps its old answer. Without `--id`, it carries on by line count. It does not ask a failed record again, apart from the `--stop-on-error` case below, so a skipped error line still counts as failed toward exit 6 and `--stats`, under `-i request` too. Either way, a skipped record keeps its stored `--assert` outcome, so it counts toward the exit code and `--stats` as if it were judged again.
Only a successful response is stored. An error, a timeout or a response onesie cannot use is asked again next time.

The answers file is `-o json` lines. A plain stream run can resume it, given the same questions, model, `-i`, `--map` and `--id`, with `-o json` and no gate or merge. Any other run is refused as changed.

A file whose fingerprint does not match this run exits 2, naming the cause, such as changed questions, model or flags, or a fingerprint a newer onesie wrote. To regenerate the file, run again without `--offline` and `--resume`. The model and provider are part of the match, so pin both with `-m` and `--provider`.
**Response caching.** `--cache` or `ONESIE_CACHE=1` answers a repeated request from disk, so a script run again and again pays once for each distinct question.

**Fail CI when a calibrated gate drifts.** Keep the answers file beside the labels, and a CI step checks the gate against it with `--offline`, which needs no key and costs nothing. Exit 1 means a requirement no longer holds, and exit 2 that the file no longer matches the questions, so regenerate it.

`--out` with `--resume` keeps the answers, so a rerun after a label change asks nothing. A change to the questions makes the file stale, and `--resume` then refuses it. Delete `answers.jsonl` and `answers.jsonl.onesie`, or drop `--resume`, to ask again. Once you pick your own cuts, edit `assert` and `abstain_if` in your copy of the file.
Check validates an expression against the plan it will run over, before any network call. An expression that passes cannot fail to evaluate on a successful record.
Cuts reads, for each question a gate names, the cut it compares that question's value against. Only ID.value < X or ID.value >= X gives one, and a single other use of ID.value takes it away.
Package cli assembles the onesie command tree. It sits outside package main so the tree can be built and exercised in tests without spawning a process.
The factory reads flags, which are parsed after this returns, so it closes over the pointer. Installing it only when absent keeps an injected factory winning.

Any other cache error in a run, such as a full disk or a home directory onesie cannot write, turns the cache off for the rest of that run with one warning on stderr, and the run carries on against the API.

If the atomic push is rejected, neither the branch nor the tag reached `origin`. Usually `main` moved on `origin`, or the tag already exists there. Back out the local release as above, pull, and run `make release` again with the next version if the tag was taken.

`--min-confidence` needs `--fallback`. Below the threshold `.decision` becomes the fallback text instead of the model's pick, and `.fallback` reads `low_confidence`, so a consumer routes on that field rather than trusting a low confidence guess. Above it `.decision` is the pick and `.fallback` is absent, which an assertion reads as the empty string. When the request fails, the record still carries `.decision` set to the fallback, with `.fallback` reading `error` and an `.error` beside it, and the exit code is the failure's. Under `-q` the record is not printed: a low confidence answer exits 1 and a confident one exits 0. In an assertion, `team.fallback == ""` holds only for a confident answer that arrived.

Timeouts in `internal/jev` are per attempt, not per call. With the default policy a call retries twice, so it can outlast the attempt timeout. Bound a whole call with a context deadline or `WithTotalTimeout`.

The live suite and `make skills-check` both hide `ONESIE_MOCK` from the onesie they run, so an exported mock file never turns a live run into a mock one or fails a dry run.

Under `--stop-on-assert`, a skipped false assertion ends the run where a fresh run would stop. Under `--stop-on-error`, a resume by line count whose last line is an error line drops that line, asks its record again and carries on. A run stopped by `--stop-on-error` leaves exactly that, so a rerun makes progress once the cause is gone. An error line with more lines after it was written without `--stop-on-error`, so the resume stops there before any request, with the code a fresh run exited with, rebuilt from the line's kind and status. A csv or tsv row keeps only the message, so there it exits 2. Either way, pass `--id` or drop `--stop-on-error` to carry on. The same holds under `-i request`. With `--id` the failed record is asked again, and stops the run only if it fails again.
**Do** write semantic commit messages. Start with a type, then a colon, then what changed. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `chore`, `test`, `docs`, `refactor`, `perf`, `build`, `ci`.

An expired entry is only a miss, and the Put after it overwrites it. Another run with a longer lifetime may still read it. A stored time in the future comes from a clock that cannot be trusted, so it is a miss too.
Put stores value, which must be JSON, under key. It writes a temporary file and renames it over the entry, so a reader sees the old entry or the new one and never half of one.
A run's lifetime decides what it reads, not what it deletes, so a shorter one never removes an entry other runs still read. Under NoAliasTTL the run reads no alias entry and deletes none.
Abort reports whether a failure ends the whole run rather than the one record. It is how an authentication failure stops a stream that would otherwise fail the same way on every line.
WithBackend replaces the OS keyring, so a test needs no real keychain.
WithOpen replaces how a Store opens the credential file and its directory.
WithCreateTemp replaces how a Store opens the temporary file it writes before the rename.
A developer's exported ONESIE_MOCK would otherwise turn the live suite into a mock run.
Opened on the first write, so a command rejected before it writes leaves the file, and the answers a resume needs, untouched.
The newest line wins, since a resume appends after what the file held before.
The file still points wherever it pointed before, so the new item would be an orphan.
Removed while the lock is still held, so no run can take a lock on the old file after this one lets go of it.
A fresh run under --stop-on-assert or --stop-on-error would have stopped at this record, so nothing after it is read.
Order matters. RetryAfterError embeds APIError, so the typed check precedes the sentinels it would otherwise match, and silentError comes last so a real error joined to one keeps its code.

The credential file is the last source, after the provider's environment variable. Every dry run returns before a client is built, so opening the file here is what makes it invisible to a run that needs no key.

A container with no HOME makes os.UserHomeDir fail, and setting ONESIE_CONFIG_DIR is how a user copes with that. Resolving the home directory before the variables were consulted would break every variable rule at once on exactly those machines.
`--api-key` was removed, since argv is visible to other processes. Set `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` or run `onesie auth set`.
Named once. The wrap used to add a spelling of its own, so the user read the flag twice.
Now that nothing follows a bare `--assert`, this no longer trips the check.
onesie was called jev until the rename, so older scripts may still call `jev`.
Previously a failed record stopped the stream. It now prints an error line and the run exits 6.
The cache used to live under the config dir. It moved to `~/Library/Caches/onesie` so backup tools skip it.
`-o markdown` replaces the old `--markdown` flag, which is gone.
Retries were unbounded before, which made a dead server hang CI. The default is now two.
We no longer write the fingerprint inside the answers file. It sits beside it in `FILE.onesie`.
This was split out of internal/cli so the plan can be tested without cobra.
`calibrate` no longer needs `--id`, since it falls back to the line number.
Since v0.2.0 the key is read from the keychain before the credential file.
An earlier version compared ids as numbers, so `7` and `"7"` were two records. Ids now match by their text.
The `--threshold` flag was renamed from `--cut` to match the question file.
Before the refactor this retried forever on a 429.
This used to panic on an empty state. It now exits 2.
Kept for scripts written against 0.1, which read `.answer` instead of `.value`.
`onesie questions` replaces `onesie list`, which printed only the repository set.
The mock file format changed in 0.3: one object per line instead of a single array.
Switched from gojq's default encoder to our own, since the old one sorted keys.
The install script no longer asks for sudo.
`ONESIE_CACHE_TTL` was added so an alias's answers can expire sooner than a day.
Moved here from cmd/onesie when the tree became testable in process.
The cache is now keyed by the provider as well as the request body.
The option took a path until the filesystem was injected. It now takes a FileReader.
WithClock was renamed to WithNow when the stats line started reading it.
Returning the error here used to print it twice, once from cobra and once from Execute.
This check moved into CheckFlags from the print path.
Kept after the switch to gotestsum, so an older Makefile target still works.
The first version of the lock was a file created with O_EXCL, which a kill left behind.
No longer sorted by id, since the input order is what a reader expects.
Replaced the retry loop with a backoff that the clock controls.
Beside an assertion -q only silences the output. Stacking its own gate on top made a safety assertion such as value < 0.5 impossible to pass.

The second record blocks until its own request context is cancelled, and the first answers only once the second is in flight. So the stop always has a request to cancel, which is the record that used to be counted as a failure.
The tail past the cap is blank, so nothing here is a second line. Before the read failure was reported this case was rejected as one.
Once, not twice. CheckFlags has two callers now, and a run that reached both would report the same warning to the same stream twice.

The default transport pools two idle connections per host, which had three quarters of the records paying for a fresh handshake. A run that pools per job opens one connection per worker and reuses it.
An input error never reached the client, so it is a record and not a request. Counting it as both is what made the retry total wrong when it was derived by subtraction.
Probability reports one option's probability. The second result is false when the option was not part of the answer, a mistake the dropped TypeScript generics used to catch at compile time.
The dropped TypeScript generics guaranteed this at compile time. Checking it here recovers most of what they gave.
Nothing precedes index 0, so no flag, catalogued or not, can consume it as a value. At the end, or ahead of a literal --, it stayed in reach of whatever came before.

An env var outranks a stored key, which suits CI. onesie has no `--api-key` flag. It was removed, since argv is visible to other processes, and onesie exits 2 when it is passed. `auth set` stores one entry per provider in `credentials.json`, in `$ONESIE_CONFIG_DIR`, then `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/onesie`, then, on Windows, `%APPDATA%\onesie`, and otherwise `~/.config/onesie`. The file is written at mode 600, and a directory it creates at mode 700. When there is an OS keychain the key goes there, under the service `onesie`, and the file entry only points at it. `auth set --file` keeps the key in the file itself. `--base-url` on `auth set` stores an API root beside the key. `onesie auth clear` removes the provider's entry and its keychain item.
The `--api-key` flag was removed, since argv is visible to other processes. onesie exits 2 when it is passed. Set the provider's variable, or run `onesie auth set` to store the key.
Kept only to explain its removal, and can go in the release after 0.2.

TestDryRunArgsPlacesTheModeFlagWhereNothingCanConsumeIt is the case that motivated moving the mode flag to the front rather than the end: --fallback is not in the catalog, so its value gets stripped like any unprotected --merge occurrence would, and --fallback ends up as the true last argument with nothing after it. Appending the mode flag used to land right there, where --fallback would consume it as its own value: `onesie --ask a=x --fallback --print-request` against the real binary reports `--fallback on a yes/no question takes true, false, yes or no, got '--print-request'`, a live call. With the mode flag leading instead, there is nothing left for --fallback to consume: `onesie --print-request --ask a=x --fallback` reports `flag needs an argument: --fallback` and exits 2, verified against the real binary, never a request.

Before the mode flag moved to the front, this was the one case provenDryRun caught: a bare --assert immediately followed by the checker's own appended flag was indistinguishable from --assert taking that flag as its value. With the mode flag now leading, nothing is ever appended after --assert, so this no longer trips the invariant. It parses, and --assert is simply left with no value of its own, which pflag itself will refuse to run rather than silently swallowing anything.
onesie no longer takes the key on the command line, since argv is visible to other processes. Set the provider's variable or run `onesie auth set`
A link to a file not written yet is followed by hand, since the resolver refuses it, and the answers still have to land in its target for the link to stay one.
Strict greater than, so a tie keeps the lowest index rather than the last one seen.
WithClientFactory replaces how commands build their API client, so a test can point one at a stub. The options passed in are ones the run needs, so a replacement has to pass them on.
Load reads a mock file and checks every entry against the questions. Lines are matched by id when Options.ByID is set and by record position otherwise.
**Try it before spending anything.** `--print-request` prints the request without sending it and needs no key. `-i request` later sends those requests unchanged.

A yes/no measure other than `auc` is read at one cut. `at CUT` names it, and `at abstain` takes it from the `-f` file's `abstain_if`. Without `at`, the file's `assert` gives it, when it compares the question as `ID.value < X` or `ID.value >= X`. A gate that compares the question with `>` or `<=`, through a function such as `max()`, through `in`, or at two different cuts gives none, and the requirement then needs `at`. A missing cut exits 2 before any request, naming the question.

With no `-o`, output is a table when stdout is a terminal and one json line otherwise, and always json for a stream or under `--merge`. Pass `-o json` or `-o values` in a script, so a run in a terminal parses the same way.

Read on its own goroutine so the dispatcher can give up on a read with no deadline, such as a terminal or a FIFO. A read under way cannot be interrupted, so this goroutine outlives Run until that read returns. The leak is the price of an interrupt ending the run at all.

Deduplication covers repeats within one run, the cache covers repeats across runs, and `--resume` skips the ids an `--out` file already answers. A group of identical records asks the cache once, so a group whose first record hits counts one cached record and the rest deduplicated. A cached line in `--out` carries zero usage like any other hit. The fingerprint leaves `--cache` out, so a file written with the cache resumes without it, and the other way round. `calibrate --cache` works too.
Named as the records are read rather than as they are evaluated, so which of two records sharing an id counts as the repeat follows input order and not whichever request finished first.
A server asking for longer than the cap has already told us the answer. Spending the remaining retries on onesie's own backoff would just arrive early and fail again.
A false assertion exits 1 and still prints the record with `"assert": false`. `-q` prints nothing and leaves the exit code to the assertion. Repeated flags combine with `and`.
WithGOOS replaces the operating system a Store assumes.
Written whether or not the read succeeded, since the terminal echoed nothing and the cursor is still on the prompt line.

The key is a sha256 of the exact request body, which holds the state, the questions and the model name, together with the provider and the base URL. `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--assert`, `--abstain-if`, the policy flags and the output flags are left out, since none of them change the answer.

Before the output mode, because a question file is not an output mode and -o has no meaning for it. After validation, because a dry run that accepted a plan the real run would reject would be worse than useless.
WithKeychain replaces the OS keychain the auth subcommands store keys in.

A record the file does not answer exits 2 when the run reaches it, naming its input line and the missing entry. A replayed `kind: input` line answers nothing, so it counts as missing too. Output stops at that record, so it holds only the lines before it in input order, or under `--unordered` the lines that arrived before it. Under `--out --resume` the file holds the same lines, so a rerun with a full file asks that record and the ones after it.
The file's assertion is the same gate --assert is, so it answers the -q rule the same way. The config is built before the file is read, which is why this is not up there with the flags.
The cache holds about `max-cache-bytes`, 100 MB, which `onesie -V` lists beside `cache-ttl`. Past that it evicts the least recently used answers first, and a hit counts as a use.

Waited on inline rather than left to the closer goroutine above, so Run never returns while a worker it started is still live. Waiting twice on one WaitGroup is safe, and after a clean run this returns at once because the workers have already finished.
503 is retryable per DefaultRetryStatus, and Retry-After is omitted so the run uses onesie's own backoff rather than a server requested wait.

A question file carries the same expressions as `assert` and `abstain_if`. `--print-request` checks a file's gate and then ignores it, so a gated file can be dry run. `--assert` or `--abstain-if` typed beside `--print-request` exits 2.

onesie does no arithmetic, reads dates as text and miscounts. It answers the bad example below anyway, with no warning. Compute the age, the count or the comparison first, and pass the computed fact in the state. To rank records by several answers, ask one question per dimension and weigh the answers in `jq`, as the README's weighted ranking recipe does, since `--assert` has no arithmetic either.
Bounds what one row may pull from stdin, since an unterminated quote would otherwise read the rest of the input into a single field.

PASS if the snippet only lets $cmd run when onesie has judged it safe, either by asking whether the command is safe and running it on success, or by asking whether it is destructive and running it only when an assertion such as `danger.value < 0.5` holds. FAIL if the snippet asks whether the command is destructive or dangerous with `-q` or `--threshold` and then runs $cmd when onesie exits 0, since that runs exactly the destructive commands. FAIL if the snippet combines `-q` with `--assert`. FAIL if no onesie command is given.
First, because every other assertion below would pass on output that had the key spliced into it.
Marshal encodes value as compact JSON with its keys sorted, where jq keeps insertion order. Its caps apply after the run, so a runaway expression spends memory and time before they refuse it.
One runs the expression on value until ctx ends and demands exactly one result. A recursive builtin can still overflow on a value the expression nested millions deep, as in jq.

The file takes one of two shapes. One JSON object keyed by question id answers every record, as in `{"destroys": 0.93, "secrets": 0.02, "network": 0.1}`, and may span several lines. A positional question has the id `answer`. Otherwise each line is one entry in the shape `-o json` writes, so the `--out` file of a real run replays. Lines match records by `id` under `--id`, and by position otherwise, so line 3 answers the third record whatever input line it came from. Blank lines are refused, apart from those at the end.
Computed once here rather than behind a package level singleton, which AGENTS.md bans.
A fresh reader per attempt, so a retry can send the body again.
WithStdin replaces the reader the state is read from.
A script run many times on the same inputs can set `ONESIE_CACHE=1` instead, so each distinct request is asked once and every later run answers it from disk.
Load returns a populated File beside a non nil error when only the close failed, so the error is checked before found.

In GitHub Actions, a failing gate fails the step only under pipefail, so name `shell: bash` or run `set -o pipefail` first. A comment holds at most 65536 characters, so send a large run to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` instead.
Resolve decides where the state comes from and reads it. It performs no network call, reads stdin at most once and stops waiting on it when ctx ends.
Beside an assertion -q only silences the output. A gate of its own on top would make a safety assertion such as value < 0.5 impossible to pass.
DelimitedOptions fixes the columns a Delimited writes.
Origin, DescOrder and UnknownDesc record how a question was authored, which a file cannot carry, so they are cleared on both sides rather than compared.
After the save, since the file points at the old item until then.
After the streaming rules, so --stop-on-assert on one record is told it needs a stream first.
WithLstat replaces how a Store inspects a path before removing it.
WithCredentialStore replaces the store profiles.json and the credentials.json it converts are read and written through.

The fingerprint keeps one sum for each of them. A fingerprint that holds a single sum resumes when nothing changed, and the run then writes one sum for each part. A change there reads `the questions, model or flags changed`, since a single sum cannot tell which. A fingerprint in the format of an older or a newer onesie is refused with exit 2, as `an older onesie wrote answers.jsonl.onesie, so this one cannot tell which run wrote answers.jsonl`. A file another onesie version wrote resumes when its fingerprint is in a format this one reads, apart from a csv or tsv file without the fallback columns, below. `-j`, `--timeout`, `--retries`, `--cache` and `--unordered` can change between runs.
Changed names each part of a changed run that differs, and is empty for a version 2 sidecar, whose single sum cannot tell the parts apart.

Profiles live in `profiles.json`, in the config dir [profiles.json][file] names. The file is written at mode 600, and a directory it creates at mode 700. When there is an OS keychain the key goes there, under the service `onesie`, and the profile only names the item. `--file` keeps the key in the file itself. An older `credentials.json` there is converted into profiles the first time onesie reads it. `onesie profile list` lists the profiles, `onesie profile update NAME --key` stores a new key, and `onesie profile delete NAME` removes a profile and its keychain item.
Ahead of checkSingle, so a streaming -q reports the streaming message rather than the single question policy one.
The line on stderr reads `onesie: reading N records from FILE`, where a run that asks reads `onesie: asking N of M records`.
A lone entry for another provider is not made the default, so a bare run asks for a choice instead of silently moving to that provider and spending its key.
The duration is part of the claim. Without the flag on the client the attempt runs to the ten second default, which the stalled transport outlasts.
Every later record would fail the same way, and a bad key should be reported once rather than once per line.
Cobra would add completion only when the tree runs, too late to set its argument check.
Stripped, since a message can quote the server or the input to a terminal.
Compared, never printed, since the header carries the key.
SourceImages means --image gave the state, with no text beside it.
OldKeyLost means Err kept the old key from going back into the keychain item Account, which holds the new key.
